lessons.title: Daily Routine and Observation
lessons.body:
Start your day with ostriches before sunrise. Walk the perimeter fence firstâcheck for holes, loose wires, or predator tracks. Ostriches are curious and will test fences; a single break can mean lost birds. Then move to the water troughs. An adult ostrich drinks 10â15 litres daily, more in heat. Clean troughs with a stiff brush and fresh water; dirty water spreads disease fast. Next, observe each bird from a distance. Look for droppings: normal is firm, dark, and well-formed. Runny or bloody droppings mean illness. Count the birdsâif one is missing, search immediately. Ostriches hide when sick or stressed.

Feeding comes next. A mature ostrich eats 2â3 kg of feed per day. In Africa, a good mix is 50% lucerne (alfalfa) hay, 30% maize meal, and 20% commercial ostrich pellet. Add limestone grit for calcium. Feed in troughs, not on the ground, to prevent worm eggs. Watch how they eat: a bird that hangs back or pecks weakly may have a throat injury or infection.

Midday, check shade and dust baths. Ostriches need shade in temperatures above 30Â°C. A simple shade cloth or tree cover works. Dust baths help control lice and ticksâprovide a shallow pit with dry sand and wood ash. If birds are panting heavily or holding wings out, they are heat-stressed. Act immediately: sprinkle water on their legs and increase airflow.

Afternoon: inspect legs and feet. Look for swelling, cuts, or scaly leg mites. A lame ostrich cannot breed or gain weight. Treat minor wounds with iodine. Check eyes for dischargeâa sign of avian influenza or sinusitis.

Evening: secure all gates. Count birds again. Record everything in a notebook: feed eaten, water consumed, any abnormal behaviour, deaths. This daily log is your early warning system. In Africa, where vet services may be far, your eyes are the best medicine.

lessons.title: Handling and Restraint Techniques
lessons.body:
Ostriches are strong and can kick forward with enough force to break a human leg. Never handle them alone. Always work in pairs, with one person as a distraction and the other as the handler. Wear long sleeves, heavy trousers, and steel-toe boots. A kick from a 120 kg bird can kill.

For moving a single ostrich, use a 'hood' or a dark cloth over the head. This calms them because they think it is night. A simple burlap sack works. Approach from the side, never from the frontâthey kick forward. Place the hood quickly and firmly. Then guide the bird by holding the base of the neck with one hand and the body with the other. Do not pull feathers; that causes pain and stress.

For restraint, use a 'crush' or a narrow race. A V-shaped trough made of poles works well. Lead the bird in, then close the head gate. For leg examination, two people lift the bird's leg gentlyânever twist. For beak trimming, use a small angle grinder with a sanding disc. Trim only the tip; cutting too deep causes bleeding.

For injections, restrain the bird in the crush. The best site is the breast muscle (pectoral). Use a 1.5-inch needle. For oral medication, use a stomach tubeânever force a bottle into the beak; they can choke.

In Africa, many farmers use a 'trip' method: a rope around the legs to make the bird sit. This is riskyâit can break bones. Avoid it. Instead, build a simple crush from local timber. It costs little and saves injuries.

Always have a escape route for yourself. If the bird panics, let it go. Never corner an ostrich. Handle only when necessary: for vaccinations, moving to new camps, or health checks. The less you handle, the calmer your birds. Record every handling eventâdate, reason, and any injuryâso you can improve your technique.

lessons.title: Stress Reduction and Welfare
lessons.body:
Stress kills ostriches silently. A stressed bird stops eating, loses weight, and gets sick. In Africa, common stressors are loud noises, dogs, strangers, and sudden changes in routine. Keep your farm quiet. Do not allow radios or shouting near the camps. Train your dogs to stay away.

Provide plenty of space. An adult ostrich needs at least 250 square metres per bird in a camp. Overcrowding causes fighting and feather pecking. Provide visual barriersâstacks of hay or shade clothâso birds can escape each other. Separate bulls (males) during breeding season; they fight for dominance.

Shade and dust baths are essential. In hot African summers, ostriches need shade from 11am to 4pm. A simple roof of thatch or corrugated iron works. Dust baths help them cool and remove parasites. Make a pit 2m x 2m with dry sand and ash. Refresh monthly.

Feed and water must be consistent. Change feed gradually over 7 days if you switch brands. Sudden changes cause digestive upset. Always provide clean waterâa thirsty ostrich is a stressed ostrich.

Handle birds calmly. Move slowly and speak softly. Never chase them. Use a flag or stick to guide, not to hit. If a bird is injured, isolate it in a quiet pen with food and water. Minimise visitors.

Welfare also means humane slaughter. If culling, use a captive bolt pistol followed by bleeding. Never cut the throat of a conscious bird.

Monitor stress signs: panting, wing drooping, pacing, and aggression. If you see these, find the cause. Often it is a predator at night, a broken water pipe, or a new person. Fix it fast. Happy ostriches grow faster and lay more eggs. Your profit depends on their comfort.

lessons.title: Seasonal Management: Heat and Cold Stress
lessons.body:
Ostriches adapt to many climates, but extremes cost you money. In Africa, heat is the bigger killer. When temperatures rise above 35Â°C, ostriches pant, hold wings out, and reduce feed intake. They can die from heat stroke.

Heat management: Provide shadeâtrees, shade cloth, or a simple roof. Orient shade east-west so it blocks midday sun. Misters or sprinklers on the roof help. Wet the ground in the shade; evaporation cools the air. Feed early morning and late evening when it is cool. Add electrolytes to water (1 teaspoon salt + 1 teaspoon baking soda per 10 litres). Never handle birds in the heat of the day.

Cold management: Ostriches can handle cold down to -5Â°C if dry and wind-free. But chicks and sick birds suffer. In cold areas like the Highveld, provide windbreaksâbales of hay or mud walls. Bedding of dry straw keeps them off cold ground. Increase feed by 10% in winter; they burn energy to stay warm. Ensure water does not freezeâcheck twice daily.

Rainy season: Mud causes foot rot and slipping. Provide raised dry areas with gravel or wood chips. Move feed troughs to high ground. Wet feathers lose insulation; provide a dry shelter.

Dust storms: Common in Sahel. Provide a windbreak of trees or a solid fence. Keep dust baths covered to prevent eye infections.

Seasonal checklist: In hot months, check water 3 times daily. In cold months, check for frostbite on toes. In rains, check for diarrhoea. Adjust feed: more energy in winter, more protein in breeding season. Record daily temperatures and bird behaviour. After one year, you will know your farm's pattern. Act before the stress, not after.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Production and Health
lessons.body:
You cannot manage what you do not measure. A simple notebook and pen are enough. Record every day: date, temperature, feed given (kg), water consumed (litres), number of eggs laid, number of birds, and any sick or dead birds.

For each bird, keep an individual card. Write its tag number, age, sex, and weight. Record vaccinations (date, vaccine name, dose). Record any illness: symptoms, treatment, and outcome. If a bird dies, note the cause if known. This helps you spot patternsâe.g., three birds died after a cold snap.

Production records: For breeding, record mating dates, egg collection dates, and which hen laid which egg (if you can identify). Hatch rates tell you if your male is fertile. If less than 60% of eggs hatch, check male-to-female ratio (1:2 is ideal) or nutrition.

Financial records: Write down all costsâfeed, vet, labour, fencingâand all incomeâegg sales, chick sales, meat, feathers. At the end of the month, subtract costs from income. If you are losing money, look at your records to find why. Maybe feed is too expensive, or you are losing too many chicks.

Use a simple spreadsheet on a phone if you have one. Apps like KoboCollect or even WhatsApp notes work. But paper is fine if kept dry.

At the end of each season, review your records. Which camp had the most disease? Which feed gave the best weight gain? Which hen laid the most eggs? Use this to make decisions: cull poor layers, change feed, or move camps.

In Africa, many farmers fail because they do not know their numbers. A record book is your farm's memory. It turns guesswork into profit.

lessons.title: Culling and Replacement Decisions
lessons.body:
Culling means removing birds that are not profitable. It is not cruelâit is good management. Replace them with better birds.

When to cull: A hen that lays fewer than 20 eggs per year (good hens lay 40â60) should be culled. A male that is infertile (less than 60% hatch rate) should be culled. Birds with chronic illness, lameness, or deformitiesâcull. Aggressive birds that injure othersâcull. Old birds: ostriches can live 40 years, but production drops after 10â12 years. Cull at 10 years for meat or leather.

How to cull: Use a captive bolt pistol to stun, then bleed out. Do it away from other birds to reduce stress. If you cannot do it yourself, hire a trained slaughterman. Never sell a sick bird at marketâit spreads disease and gives you a bad name.

Replacement: Keep your best 10% of hens and 5% of males as breeders. Select for: high egg production, good fertility, fast growth, and calm temperament. Buy new bloodlines every 3â4 years to avoid inbreeding. In Africa, look for local breeds like the South African Black or Kenyan Red. They are adapted to heat and local diseases.

Record keeping helps: Use your records to identify your best and worst birds. Tag them clearly. When you cull, note the reason. Over time, your flock improves.

Do not keep a bird out of pity. Every mouth costs feed. If it does not pay, it must go. But do it humanely. Plan culling for cool mornings. Have everything readyâknives, stun gun, bleeding area. After culling, process the meat quickly or sell to a butcher. Leather is valuableâsalt it and sell to a tannery.

Replace immediately so your production does not drop. Buy healthy chicks from a reputable hatchery. Quarantine new birds for 30 days before mixing. Culling is a tool for progress.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do when starting your daily ostrich routine?
quiz.explanation: Checking the fence first prevents escapes and predator entry before other tasks.

quiz.q: How much water does an adult ostrich drink per day?
quiz.explanation: Adult ostriches need 10â15 litres daily, more in hot weather.

quiz.q: What does runny or bloody droppings indicate?
quiz.explanation: Runny or bloody droppings are a sign of disease or digestive problems.

quiz.q: Why should feed be given in troughs, not on the ground?
quiz.explanation: Ground feeding increases the risk of ingesting worm eggs and parasites.

quiz.q: What is a sign of heat stress in ostriches?
options: B) Panting and holding wings out
quiz.explanation: Panting and wing-holding are classic signs of overheating.

quiz.q: Why should you never handle an ostrich alone?
options: B) They can kick hard enough to break bones
quiz.explanation: Ostriches have powerful forward kicks that can cause serious injury or death.

quiz.q: What is a safe method to calm an ostrich for handling?
options: B) Put a hood over its head
quiz.explanation: A hood or dark cloth over the head calms the bird by simulating night.

quiz.q: Where is the best site for injecting an ostrich?
quiz.explanation: The breast muscle (pectoral) is the safest and most common injection site.

quiz.q: What should you avoid when restraining an ostrich?
quiz.explanation: Pulling feathers causes pain and stress; handle the body and neck instead.

quiz.q: How much space does an adult ostrich need in a camp?
quiz.explanation: At least 250 square metres per bird prevents overcrowding and fighting.

quiz.q: What is a common stressor for ostriches in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Loud noises, dogs, and strangers are common stressors that can harm health.

quiz.q: How should you change an ostrich's feed?
quiz.explanation: Gradual change over 7 days prevents digestive upset.

quiz.q: What is a sign of stress in ostriches?
quiz.explanation: Pacing, wing drooping, and aggression are common stress indicators.

quiz.q: At what temperature do ostriches start to suffer heat stress?
quiz.explanation: Above 35Â°C, ostriches pant and reduce feed intake, risking heat stroke.

quiz.q: What should you add to water during heat stress?
quiz.explanation: Electrolytes help replace lost salts and maintain hydration.

quiz.q: How can you protect ostriches from cold?
options: A) Provide windbreaks and dry bedding
quiz.explanation: Windbreaks and dry straw bedding keep them warm and dry.

quiz.q: What is a sign of foot rot in rainy season?
quiz.explanation: Mud causes foot rot, seen as swelling and bad smell.

quiz.q: Why keep daily records?
options: B) To spot patterns and make decisions
quiz.explanation: Records help identify disease trends, feed efficiency, and profit.

quiz.q: What should you record for each bird?
options: B) Tag number, age, sex, weight, health events
quiz.explanation: Individual records track growth, vaccinations, and illness for better management.

quiz.q: What does a hatch rate below 60% suggest?
options: B) Male infertility or poor nutrition
quiz.explanation: Low hatch rate often means male infertility or nutritional deficiencies.

quiz.q: How often should you review production records?
quiz.explanation: Seasonal review helps make decisions on culling, feed, and camp rotation.

quiz.q: What is culling?
quiz.explanation: Culling removes birds that are not productive or healthy to improve flock quality.

quiz.q: When should a hen be culled?
options: B) If she lays fewer than 20 eggs per year
C) If she is 2 years old
quiz.explanation: Hens laying fewer than 20 eggs per year are not profitable and should be culled.

quiz.q: What is the ideal male-to-female ratio for breeding ostriches?
quiz.explanation: One male to two females ensures good fertility without fighting.

quiz.q: How should culling be done humanely?
options: B) Captive bolt stunning then bleeding
quiz.explanation: Stunning with a captive bolt followed by bleeding is the humane method.

quiz.q: How often should you introduce new bloodlines?
quiz.explanation: New bloodlines every 3â4 years prevent inbreeding and maintain vigour.

quiz.q: What should you do with a sick bird at market?
quiz.explanation: Selling sick birds spreads disease and damages your reputation.

quiz.q: What is a good shade orientation for ostrich camps?
quiz.explanation: East-west orientation blocks midday sun most effectively.

quiz.q: What is a dust bath used for?
quiz.explanation: Dust baths with sand and ash help control lice and ticks and aid cooling.

quiz.q: How many eggs per year does a good hen lay?
quiz.explanation: A productive hen lays 40â60 eggs per year under good management.
